newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem wants U.S. beef action for patent progress.
newsitem.headline: Menem wants U.S. beef action for patent progress.

text.p: Argentina will address the United States' concerns about confidentiality for intellectual property in return for U.S. action on Argentine beef imports, Argentine President Carlos Menem said Monday.

His Peronist government had hoped Congress would pass a confidentiality bill last week to supplement the patents law passed in March by forbidding dissemination of information on a new product for a five-year period after it is registered.
But the opposition objected to the Peronists' last-minute attempt for the law to come into effect from January 1, 1997 rather than 2001, and the debate was postponed to this week.

Menem, speaking to a small group of foreign journalists on the eve of his visit to New York and Washington, promised to have in his hand a definitive version of the bill by the time he meets President Bill Clinton in Washington Thursday.
"We are expecting a draft from the relevant committee in ...the Chamber of Deputies to take to the United States what is going to be the definitive version of the law," he said.
Peronist deputies and government officials are due to meet Tuesday to plan their strategy to ensure the bill is passed in Congress Wednesday, following last week's setback.

Patent protection, especially for pharmaceutical exports, is the biggest sticking-point in otherwise fluid relations between Washington and Buenos Aires. Senior Clinton aide Thomas McLarty said here late last month his government was "frankly disappointed" by March's patent law.

Menem said in return for addressing such concerns, "we for our part are going to ask the United States to meet all commitments on meat," which he said includes approval for imports of 20,000 tonnes a year of high quality beef.

Argentine beef was banned for decades in world markets, including the strategically important Unites States because of concerns about foot-and-mouth disease. But its cattle herd of 50 million has not had an outbreak for more than two years.

"Argentina now meets all the health requirements. It has wiped out foot-and-mouth for good and the problem of Mad Cow disease doesn't exist, so we are in a condition to sell our meat not just in the United States, but all over the world," said Menem.
